meta.title: Who really said "Republicans buy sneakers, too"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Never said in public: the line first reached print in 1995 as "Republicans buy shoes, too." Jordan denied it for years, then owned it in 2020.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Republicans buy sneakers, too'?
meta.ogDescription: Michael Jordan's most quoted sentence has no 1990 record. It reached print in 1995 as "shoes," not "sneakers" — and he denied it until The Last Dance.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: b. 1963 · NBA guard, 1984–2003 · six titles with the Chicago Bulls
answer.sourceLine: Jordan has acknowledged the remark — in The Last Dance (2020) he said he made it “in jest” on a team bus — but there is no contemporaneous record of it. The sentence did not reach print until 1995, in Sam Smith’s Second Coming, where it appears secondhand and in a different form: “Republicans buy shoes, too.” The “sneakers” wording that became famous is a later rendering.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Second Coming: The Strange Odyssey of Michael Jordan
1990 North Carolina Senate race, Helms vs. Gantt

source.excerpt: And, as he later told a friend, “Republicans buy shoes, too.”
trail: November 6, 1990 — the race. Jesse Helms holds his North Carolina Senate seat against Harvey Gantt, the former Charlotte mayor, 52.58% to 47.39%. Jordan, the state’s most famous son, makes no endorsement. Election record ↗

1995 — the line reaches print. Its first known appearance is in the preface to Sam Smith’s Second Coming, and in a different shape: shoes, not sneakers, and secondhand — Smith writes that Jordan said it to a friend. Slate ↗

1996–1999 — it hardens into a quotation. A 1996 Richmond Times-Dispatch column carries it in the “sneakers” form; Jason Zengerle used it in The American Prospect in 1997; David Halberstam’s Playing for Keeps (1999) carried the idea as a paraphrase, without quotation marks. Nyhan’s 2005 audit ↗

2016, then 2020 — denied, then owned. Jordan’s spokeswoman tells Slate he denies ever saying it. Then, in The Last Dance, he says the opposite: it was a joke on a team bus, and he sent Gantt a contribution rather than record a PSA. ESPN ↗
source.excerptNote: The surrounding passage, quoted by Slate, has Smith describing Jordan’s tight management of his own image before turning to the Gantt–Helms race: approached about lending his name, Jordan declined, saying he was not into politics and did not really know the issues. Note the two problems for anyone citing this as the source of the famous line — the noun is shoes, and Smith attributes it not to himself but to “a friend” Jordan told.

source.rightsNote: The remark itself was spoken privately and was never published at the time, so there is no old, free-standing document behind it. Every text that records it sits inside a copyrighted modern work — Sam Smith’s Second Coming (HarperCollins, 1995) and There Is No Next (Diversion Books, 2014), and ESPN’s The Last Dance (2020) — all long after the 1931 U.S. public-domain line, so nothing here can be treated as public domain.

author.name: Michael Jordan
author.heading: Michael Jordan
author.metaLine: Born 1963 · NBA guard, 1984–2003 · six championships with the Chicago Bulls
author.bio: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963) played fifteen NBA seasons between 1984 and 2003 and won six championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was also one of the most heavily marketed athletes who has ever lived: Nike introduced the Air Jordan in 1984, and the shoe line is the reason a throwaway sentence about footwear and voters became the most-quoted thing he never said in public. For most of his playing career he declined to take political positions — a stance he revisited in 2016, when he condemned police violence and announced $1 million donations each to the Institute for Community-Police Relations and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in Sam Smith, Second Coming: The Strange Odyssey of Michael Jordan—From Courtside to Home Plate and Back Again (New York: HarperCollins, 1995), where the line reads “Republicans buy shoes, too”; the “sneakers” wording is Smith’s own in There Is No Next (Diversion Books, 2014). Michael Jordan acknowledged making the remark in The Last Dance (ESPN, 2020).
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Republicans buy sneakers, too’?” Last verified 17 Aug 2026.

copyAttribution: "Republicans buy sneakers, too." — attributed to Michael Jordan, on declining to endorse Harvey Gantt in the 1990 North Carolina Senate race against Jesse Helms. No contemporaneous record exists; the line first reached print as "Republicans buy shoes, too" in Sam Smith's Second Coming (HarperCollins, 1995), reported secondhand. Jordan acknowledged the remark — made "in jest" on a team bus — in The Last Dance (ESPN, 2020). Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What the internet gets wrong about it
misattribution.intro: The surprise here is not the speaker. Jordan says he said it. Almost everything else attached to the sentence — the wording, the room, the motive, the date it can be documented — is off.

items.why: That is how Sam Smith set it down in Second Coming in 1995, the line’s first known appearance in print. “Sneakers” is the version that spread through newspapers — and the version Smith himself switched to when he retold the story in 2014. Slate ↗

The line is usually staged as Jordan’s reply to the campaign. By his own 2020 account it was said on a team bus to Horace Grant and Scottie Pippen; the actual request reached him through his mother, who asked him to record a PSA for Gantt, and he sent a contribution instead. ESPN ↗

Smith, the only journalist who claims to have heard it, describes a joke delivered with a smile, and in 2020 called it a show of defiance at the NBA’s preference that its stars avoid politics — not a statement of commercial philosophy. Awful Announcing ↗

Nothing from the campaign itself records it. Brendan Nyhan and Jason Zengerle, writing in 2005, found the earliest printed citations to be years later and secondhand, and noted that David Halberstam — a careful reporter — carried the idea as a paraphrase without quotation marks. Nyhan, 2005 ↗

In 2016 his spokeswoman Estee Portnoy told Slate by email that Jordan denies ever saying it. In 2020 he told the opposite story on camera: “I don’t think that statement needs to be corrected because I said it in jest.” ESPN ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Jordan no longer denies the sentence — he says he said it, as a joke, on a bus. What no source can supply is a contemporaneous record of the exact words, which is why the line still travels in two versions and why “attributed” is as far as the evidence goes. Jordan’s own account, 2020 ↗

context.heading: Why one sentence about shoes has outlived the election
lead: The 1990 North Carolina Senate race was not an ordinary contest. Jesse Helms, the Republican incumbent, was running against Harvey Gantt, the former mayor of Charlotte, who would have become the state’s first Black senator; Helms’s campaign closed with the notorious “White Hands” advertisement attacking affirmative action, and he won by a little over five points. North Carolina’s most famous son stayed out of it. Slate reconstructed the whole episode in 2016 ↗

The criticism was immediate and came from inside the house. Arthur Ashe tried to talk Jordan into endorsing Gantt and later wrote that Jordan had made a mistake; Jim Brown said in 1991 that Jordan’s “main concern is the demands of corporate America”; Kareem Abdul-Jabbar said in 2015 that Jordan “took commerce over conscience.” None of them were quoting the sneakers line — it had not been printed yet. The sentence arrived afterward and became the shorthand for an argument that already existed. Slate ↗
detailsBody: Sam Smith — the one journalist who says he was there — has spent years arguing the line was misread. In 2020 he described it not as a marketing calculation but as a joke made with a smile, a show of defiance at the NBA’s preference that its stars stay clear of politics. Asked in 2016 to explain the discrepancy between his two published versions, or whether he had heard it firsthand, he declined: “It was 30 years ago.” Smith’s 2020 clarification ↗

The phrase long ago stopped belonging to the story that produced it. In 2018 the sports commentator Clay Travis used it as the title of a book, Republicans Buy Sneakers Too: How the Left Is Ruining Sports — an argument the original remark, on Smith’s telling, was not making. Wikipedia’s article on the quote ↗
context.pull: It was thrown off the cuff.

sourcesVerified.claim: The quote first appeared in Sam Smith's 1995 book Second Coming as "Republicans buy shoes, too," reported secondhand ("as he later told a friend"); Smith used the "sneakers" wording and implied firsthand hearing in his 2014 book There Is No Next; a 1996 Richmond Times-Dispatch column carried the "sneakers" form; Halberstam's Playing for Keeps (1999) paraphrased it; Jordan's spokeswoman Estee Portnoy told Slate that Jordan denies ever saying it; Gantt lost 53%-47%; Helms ran the "White Hands" ad; Arthur Ashe, Jim Brown (1991) and Kareem Abdul-Jabbar (2015) criticised Jordan; Smith said "It was 30 years ago. I'm not getting into a discussion about that."; Jordan's 2016 statement included $1m each to the Institute for Community-Police Relations and the NAACP Legal Defense Fund.

In The Last Dance, Jordan said: "I don't think that statement needs to be corrected because I said it in jest on a bus with Horace Grant and Scottie Pippen. It was thrown off the cuff. My mother asked to do a PSA for Harvey Gantt, and I said, 'Look, Mom, I'm not speaking out of pocket about someone that I don't know. But I will send a contribution to support him.' Which is what I did." Article dated May 4, 2020.

Nyhan's 2005 post (with Jason Zengerle) traces the quote: a 1996 Richmond Times-Dispatch article, Zengerle's 1997 American Prospect piece, and Halberstam's 1999 Playing for Keeps which paraphrases rather than directly quotes, without quotation marks; concludes the quote cannot be traced to a primary source and is secondhand.

Wikipedia has a dedicated article on the quote stating it first appeared in Sam Smith's 1995 book Second Coming as "Republicans buy shoes, too"; that the phrase is commonly rendered both ways; that Jordan confirmed in The Last Dance it was made in jest on a bus; and that Clay Travis titled a 2018 book Republicans Buy Sneakers Too: How the Left Is Ruining Sports.

The 1990 United States Senate election in North Carolina was held November 6, 1990; Jesse Helms defeated Harvey Gantt, former mayor of Charlotte, 52.58% to 47.39%; the Helms campaign ran a racially charged advertisement about racial quotas.

The Internet Archive holds a scan of Sam Smith, Second Coming: The Strange Odyssey of Michael Jordan--from Courtside to Home Plate and Back Again, HarperCollins Publishers, New York, 1995 (access-restricted lending copy).

Sam Smith in 2020 described Jordan's remark as a joke delivered with a smile and 'a show of defiance against the NBA's preference for its stars to stay away from political stances that could be viewed as controversial,' saying he heard it directly and that he laughed.

Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born February 17, 1963; he played 15 NBA seasons between 1984 and 2003, winning six championships with the Chicago Bulls; the Air Jordan sneaker was introduced by Nike in 1984; in 1990 Jordan declined to endorse Harvey Gantt, reportedly remarking 'Republicans buy sneakers, too'.
